name: Rolipram
lead: Rolipram is a selective phosphodiesterase-4 (PDE4) inhibitor. By slowing the breakdown of the signalling molecule cAMP, it affects inflammation and brain signalling, which is why it has been used widely as a research tool and was developed as an antidepressant.[1][2] In recovery-minded circles it is mentioned for its anti-inflammatory and memory-related effects, which proponents connect to training recovery, mood and sleep, and through them to how a person looks.

Schering AG developed rolipram as a possible antidepressant; trials found a narrow therapeutic window because doses high enough to be effective brought gastrointestinal side effects, and development ended.[1] It remains an investigational compound and the prototype for later PDE4 inhibitors such as cilomilast.[3][3]

Rolipram matters to appearance-minded readers mainly through the drug class it started. PDE4 inhibitors descended from rolipram research are now marketed as skin treatments, including apremilast for plaque psoriasis and crisaborole for atopic dermatitis, and topical roflumilast for plaque psoriasis [14]. Rolipram itself was never marketed.

chain: Proponents link this to recovery and mood
angle.text: Rolipram is discussed as an anti-inflammatory, pro-cAMP compound that people hope will support recovery and cognition, indirectly supporting training consistency and appearance.

paras: Rolipram is not a consumer product, but the enzyme it blocks is a target in skin and inflammatory disease. PDE4 is the dominant phosphodiesterase in neutrophils, eosinophils and other immune cells, and blocking it lowers their activation [4]. Drugs built on that principle are now used for visible skin conditions: apremilast (Otezla) was approved by the US FDA in 2014 for psoriatic arthritis and plaque psoriasis, crisaborole (Eucrisa) in 2016 for mild-to-moderate atopic dermatitis, and a 0.3 percent roflumilast cream (Zoryve) in 2022 for plaque psoriasis in people aged 12 and over [14].

In the recovery and cognition-focused supplement and nootropic circles where rolipram is occasionally mentioned, proponents link its anti-inflammatory and memory-related effects to training recovery, mood and sleep, and through those to physique and overall look. A 2007 T Nation thread on brain-function supplements includes a passing remark that rolipram looks promising [15]. Discussion of the compound is sparse compared with common supplements, and it is not a regulated consumer product.

PDE4 is an enzyme family that breaks down cyclic AMP; PDE4B in particular is described as a regulator of brain signalling relevant to cognition and neuroinflammation.[2] PDE4 is the dominant phosphodiesterase in immune cells such as neutrophils, eosinophils, mast cells and macrophages, where its inhibition reduces activation.[4] Rolipram is the reference compound used to study this mechanism.[3]
Reported oral bioavailability is about 75%, with liver metabolism by several CYP enzymes and an elimination half-life of about 3 hours.[1]

Rolipram was discovered and developed by Schering AG as an antidepressant candidate. Its narrow therapeutic window ended its clinical development, but it became a prototype for other companies' PDE4 programs.[1] Second-generation PDE4 inhibitors such as cilomilast were designed to retain rolipram's activity with an improved profile.[3]

Wikipedia describes rolipram as a well-characterized PDE4 inhibitor that remains widely used in research on autoimmune disease, Alzheimer disease, cognitive enhancement, spinal cord injury, asthma and COPD [1]. Radiolabelled (R)-rolipram is also used as a PET imaging tracer to map PDE4 in living brains, in registered studies that include healthy volunteers and patients with depression, Huntington disease and McCune-Albright syndrome [9].
Rolipram has no approved medical use and no ATC code; Wikipedia lists its legal status as investigational [1].

Wikipedia reports that trials showed a narrow therapeutic window: doses high enough to work brought significant gastrointestinal side effects [1]. A general account of PDE4 inhibitors states that nausea and vomiting are the most commonly implicated effects and that vomiting has been linked to inhibition of the PDE4D isoform in the area postrema of the brain, a limitation that has shaped the clinical development of the whole class [14]. Later compounds such as cilomilast were designed to improve on rolipram's profile [3].
The gastrointestinal side effects that limited the dose are the main reported adverse effect.[1]

Rolipram was tested in depression in the 1980s and early 1990s: a phase II study of its antidepressant effect, and randomized comparisons with imipramine and amitriptyline in major depression.[5][6][7] A phase II trial of rolipram in multiple sclerosis was registered in 2001, and imaging studies have used radiolabelled rolipram to measure PDE4 in the brain.[8][9]

In animals, rolipram has facilitated long-lasting long-term potentiation and memory, improved synaptic and cognitive function in an Alzheimer mouse model, and, with Schwann cells, promoted axon growth after spinal cord injury.[10][11][12] These are laboratory findings. Chemotherapy-related cognitive problems are among conditions where PDE4 inhibitors such as rolipram have been proposed for study.[13]

The antidepressant trials were run in Europe in the 1980s and early 1990s. They compared rolipram with established tricyclic antidepressants, imipramine and amitriptyline, in patients with major depression [6][7]. The multiple sclerosis phase II trial (NCT00011375, n=52, started 2001) is listed as completed [8]. No registered or published trial has examined rolipram for skin, muscle recovery or physique outcomes.

In a double-blind comparison with imipramine in 64 inpatients with major depression at six centers, imipramine was superior to rolipram toward the end of the study on the chosen outcome measure; nausea was the typical side effect of rolipram, while imipramine mainly caused anticholinergic effects [6]. In a double-blind comparison with amitriptyline in 50 hospital inpatients, amitriptyline produced a substantially greater recovery rate, about twice as many rolipram patients left the study because of lack of efficacy or adverse effects, and rolipram caused fewer anticholinergic effects but more nausea; the authors concluded that amitriptyline was more effective [7].

timeline.event: A phase II study of rolipram's antidepressant effect is published in Pharmacopsychiatry [5].
A double-blind comparison of rolipram with imipramine in major depression is reported [6].
A randomized comparison with amitriptyline in in-patient major depression is published [7].
Animal work shows rolipram facilitates long-lasting long-term potentiation and memory [10].
Rolipram improves synaptic and cognitive function in an Alzheimer mouse model, and with Schwann cells aids recovery after spinal cord injury in animals [11][12].
Apremilast, a PDE4 inhibitor, receives FDA approval for psoriatic arthritis and later plaque psoriasis [14].

card.summary: A PDE4 inhibitor studied for inflammation and cognition, discussed by some for recovery, mood and memory that support training and appearance.
card.note: Investigational only; gastrointestinal side effects limited dosing in trials.

quick.overview:
Rolipram is a PDE4 inhibitor, a compound that raises cAMP signalling. It was developed by Schering as an antidepressant and is now mostly a research tool.

People interested in recovery follow it for its anti-inflammatory and memory-related effects, which they connect to training, mood and, indirectly, appearance.
quick.mechanism: It blocks PDE4, the enzyme that breaks down cAMP, which affects immune-cell activation and brain signalling involved in memory.
quick.risks: Gastrointestinal side effects limited the doses that could be used, and development as a drug ended. It is investigational and not an approved medicine.
